## Intent
Hypothesis: compiler auto-vectorization with parallelism can approach the streaming ceiling on low-churn workloads.

## Cache saturation
At death_q=0.01, cost FALLS from 7.32 ns/p at N=10000 (past L1d spill at N≈910, within L2) to 5.71 ns/p at N=100000 (just past L2 spill at N≈58254) — overhead amortization, not a cache knee. From N=100000 through N=10000000 the curve stays FLAT at 5.88–5.94 ns/p with no rise at L2→DRAM. Death rate raises the floor without reshaping the curve: at q=0.5 the floor is 10.32–10.39 ns/p across all N, but the flat post-L2 shape persists. The L1d spill at N≈910 is not directly sampled.

## Bandwidth
Peak achieved is 12.74 GB/s at N=100000, death_q=0.01 — 42.6% of the 29.9 GB/s ceiling. At q=0.01 the algo is compute-bound (compute 65.1–65.7%, backend 28–30%, branch_flush under 5.3%). As death rate rises it shifts branch-bound: at q=0.5, N=10000000, 1 thread, branch_flush reaches 36.4% and bandwidth falls to 4.54 GB/s (15.2% of ceiling). The transition is driven by death rate, not N.

## Assembly
The compiler did not vectorize: zero vector-suffixed instructions. All FP is scalar — `fmul s5`, `fadd s5`, `fsub s5`, `fcvtzs` on single registers, with scalar loads `ldp s5, s6` and `ldr s17`. No gather (`ld1` absent). The output scatter is byte-granular: `ldrb w2, [x1]`, `add`, `csel` clamp to 0xff, `strb w2, [x1]` repeated for three bytes. This read-modify-write byte pattern explains why bandwidth caps at 43% of ceiling — byte stores cannot stream.

## Verdict
Refuted — zero vector instructions means no auto-vectorization occurred. Peak bandwidth is 12.74 GB/s = 42.6% of the 29.9 GB/s ceiling, and byte-granular `strb` scatter stores prevent streaming regardless of death rate. At q=0.5, branch_flush consumes 36.4% of cycles and bandwidth drops to 4.54 GB/s, confirming the scalar codegen cannot approach the ceiling in any regime.
